title: Meander and oxbow sketch sheet
subject: Geography
source: Seeded from geography/y10 lesson 54 (Meander and oxbow sketch sheet (portal printable))
intro: Lesson 54: Lowland river landforms: meanders, oxbow lakes, flood plains and levees (1.2c). To understand how erosion and deposition form lowland river landforms

questions.q: Explain why levees form next to the channel.
questions.a: When the river floods, it loses speed as it leaves the channel (1); the heaviest, coarsest sediment is dropped first, beside the channel (1); repeated floods build these banks up into levees (1)
questions.model: Event: a flood spreads water over the banks. Change: the water slows down. Result: heavy sediment drops first, right by the channel. Over many floods: raised banks (levees).

questions.q: State where deposition happens on a meander.

questions.a: Sideways erosion of the river banks

questions.q: Core: 'Explain the formation of an oxbow lake.' Use labelled sketches and write in the portal response box.
questions.a: Lateral erosion on outer bends narrows the neck; during a flood the river cuts through; flow takes the straighter course; deposition seals the old meander, leaving an oxbow lake
questions.model: Teacher draws sketch 1: a tight meander with arrows on the outer bends labelled 'erosion' and the neck labelled 'narrowing'.

questions.q: Extend: Compare landforms in the upper and lower course.
questions.a: Upper: V-shaped valleys, spurs, waterfalls from vertical erosion; lower: meanders, oxbows, flood plains, levees from lateral erosion and deposition; gradient and discharge differ

questions.q: Stretch: Suggest why people build on flood plains despite the risk.
questions.a: Flat, fertile land near water and transport (1); pressure for housing (1)
A meander neck is cut through
options: A meander neck is cut through

questions.q: Big question: how can a river cut itself off and leave a lake behind?
questions.a: Erosion narrows a meander neck; a flood breaks through, and deposition seals off the old loop as an oxbow lake
